Climate: The Good News

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look back on one of the most unusual and challenging periods in recent history and ask whether we're making any progress in meeting the climate change challenge.

Unique Selling Point:
With so much pessimism around right now, this piece offers a chance to look back on some of our environmental coverage for clues as to whether we're any closer to stemming the onslaught on our natural heritage. If we are, then there may be green shoots in our efforts to confront the biggest environmental challenge of them all: global warming.

Summary:
This will be both a retrospective piece and a look ahead. Through intimate cell phone video recordings from our presenters, we'll reflect on some of their more challenging environmental stories, and their hopes for a greener future. We'll also re-connect with a few of the experts and case studies interviewed on past stories, notably "Palm Oil" and "Greener on the Other Side", to see what progress they've made in continuing to champion the environmental cause.

Finally, we'll interview a South African recipient of the Newton Prize working hard to figure out how to help communities reliant on the ever-diminishing Atlantic Ocean resource.

Further information:
This piece has as its genesis a conversation with Irish Whale expert, Simon Berrow. He admitted, in as brutal an assessment I've yet encountered, that his hopes for the future are diminishing. When giving school talks, he feels inclined to apologise to the younger generation for the mess they're inheriting from their elders. The question is, do we stop at an apology or continue working towards meaningful change? Berrow argues for the latter. And for as long as their are people like him on this planet, there is hope.

Script:


UPSOUND Antonio Guterres [04:01 – 04:09] “My generation has failed in its responsibility to protect our planet. That must change.

VO: International diplomacy is known for straddling the middle ground.

UPSOUND Antonio Guterres [04:10 – 04:21] The climate emergency is a race we are losing, but it is a race we can win. The climate crisis is caused by us, but the solutions must come from us”.

VO: Not if this statement by UN Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, is anything to go by. Not when it comes to climate change. It’s something apparent in scientific circles, too.

ITV Mike Roberts [33:23] climate change is real. It's absolutely real. And people don't realize it. It's impacting them every single day.

VO: After decades spent trying to make sense of complex marine ecosystems, Professor Michael Roberts, doesn’t mince his words. An Oceanographer, he’s an eyewitness to the Climate Emergency. And if it’s solutions you’re after, he’s just the person to talk to.

Link: First, though, it’s important to understand how serious the problem is – and Professor Robert’s current research does just that. Right now, he’s focussing on this part of the Indian Ocean – an area providing food and livelihoods to tens of millions of people.

ITV Mike Roberts [10:02] “STRAP: Professor: Oceanography, NMU” there's some 60 million people who live on the shores of Eastern Africa, we call it the western Indian Ocean (CUT) And these 60 million people are pretty dependent on the ocean (CUT) for instance (CUT) people in Zanzibar and Mafia, these island areas, use fish six times a week in their diet, whereas on the mainland, it's once a week.

VO: When you consider that the population of Tanzania alone has almost doubled in the past 20 years, you get a sense of the pressure the ocean is under. But that’s not the only concern the waters here are warming.

ITV Mike Roberts [07:11] the western Indian Ocean seems to be heating up a little bit faster than many other parts of the world (CUT) our models are showing us that in 80 years or so, we're probably looking between three-and-a-half to maybe five degrees centigrade.

VO: Where the climate’s concerned, seemingly small margins can have major impacts – especially on complex ocean ecosystems. So, while that increase might not sound like much, the consequences for the people on Africa’s east coast would be profound. Warm water is nutrient poor, which means fish either die or go in search of food elsewhere – leaving locals communities with empty nets and empty pockets.

ITV Mike Roberts [12:09] we're looking in some areas, for instance, like Kenya, where you may have as much as 70 percent reduction in the fishery. So, this is serious. This is a very, very serious problem.

Link: A serious problem among many serious problems: it’s one of the sad realities of climate change that it seems to reserve its worst effects for the planet’s most marginalised communities.

VO: In another tragic twist, the 10 most food-insecure countries in the world generate just 0.08% of global CO2 – a prime greenhouse gas. Contribute little, sacrifice much. One of those countries is Mozambique.

VO: That’s where Dr. Bernadino Malawene, a scientist and researcher working closely with Professor Roberts, calls home.

ITV Bernadino Malawene [17:23] climate change is impacting in many different ways.

VO: One of the world’s least developed countries, 60% of Mozambique’s population lives along the coast – exposed to climate change and its, sometimes unexpected, impacts

ITV Bernadino Malawene [20:56] climate change affects the wind (CUT) And the wind is the other factor that brings productivity (CUT) - the wind is the rain of the ocean for (CUT) So, as much we have winds in the favourable direction and the favourable speed, we will have more production. And this heating, this climate change is changing the wind. So, we will have less favourable wind, we will have less upwelling, which is the production of the ocean, and less food for the fishers.

VO: Talking of wind and rain – Dr. Malawene’s home country gets its share of both, increasingly at the same time.

ITV Bernadino Malawene [17:23] STRAP “Marine Scientist at IIP, Mozambique” We know Mozambique is being hit by tropical cyclones every year and the intensity of these cyclones is increasing (CUT) And we can see people are losing their houses, are losing their sources of income.

VO: Scientists have long warned that climate change will make tropical cyclones more intense, bringing bigger storm surges and more rain. A rising ocean temperature is one of the reasons why.

VO: In March last year, Cyclone Idai pummelled coastal Mozambique. My colleague, Claire Mawisa, covered the aftermath.

ITV Claire Mawisa [08:34 – 08:40] We had no plan. We were just trying to document it to show people at home what was happening.

VO: Idai was the deadliest cyclone ever recorded in the South-West Indian Ocean basin. It caused severe flooding in four countries and killed 1200 people.

ITV Claire Mawisa [08:44] It overwhelmed me in a way… I was still digesting it weeks and months after returning (09:02) I couldn’t put it all together. It was a sensory overload, it was visually overwhelming, it was people… it was just so much for me to take in.

VO: But, as much as this region shows the worst impacts of climate change, it also offers reason for hope. And, at the end of a difficult year, that’s worth reflecting on.
Link: Just last month, Professor Roberts was awarded the coveted Newton Prize which recognises “teams of people making an essential contribution”. Ocean science is extremely expensive, so the 4 million rand he won will be put to good use.

VO: Professor Roberts is a shrewd fund raiser, tapping into the goodwill of donors to fund the ships and technology needed to better understand what is happening in the Western Indian Ocean. With a growing recognition of the climate crisis at least there are those putting their money where their mouths are.

ITV Mike Roberts [24:37] I guess good scientists, successful scientists who are able to run big programs and to address huge challenges like this have to be good salesmen in a way, and to convince governments that that these are very worthy projects to invest in.

VO: And that money is – in part – training a new generation of scientists like Dr. Bernadino
Malawene who, with their local knowledge and connection to the communities at risk, are providing regional governments with regional data.

ITV Bernadino Malawene [24:46] So far, the information that we are using in Mozambique is based on global models and now we are in the process of downscaling these global models to a regional application for Mozambique. And also putting more experiments, more equipment, using new technology to measure the temperature along the coast.

Link: Is there enough money and political will? Certainly not. But there is astonishing commitment to the cause from scientists like Roberts, Malawene and countless others. There’s a younger generation, too, increasingly demanding their shot at a normal future.

VO: And, armed with information, it would seem their voices are now being heard.
Ends.
